terms.gloss: foreign: of another country, as against ours
terms.comment: What belongs to other states: foreign peoples, wars and affairs. Lewis & Short set it against domesticus and noster: rēbus externīs … īnstitūtīs domesticīs, in foreign and in home affairs (Cic. Phil. 2.69).

terms.gloss: foreign: coming from abroad (people, goods, words); as a noun, a foreigner
evidence: Quint. 1.5.55: verba aut Latīna aut peregrīna sunt
terms.comment: Traupman’s word for what comes from abroad, and his noun for a foreigner, peregrīnus, peregrīna. In Rome a peregrīnus was a free resident who was not a citizen.

evidence: Nep. Eum. 7.1: sī potius ipse aliēnigena summī imperiī potīrētur
terms.comment: Very frequent in Cicero’s speeches; also used as an adjective (Lewis & Short).

terms.register: vōx cōmica: Plaut.; later Gell., Apul.
terms.comment: Ante- and post-classical (Lewis & Short); Morgan–Owens keeps it for foods and goods.

evidence: Cic. Ac. 2.48: objectā terribilī rē extrīnsecus (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: An adverb in classical Latin. Traupman gives it as an adjective, extrīnsecus, -a, -um, “from abroad”; Lewis & Short has the adjective only in late Latin (Tertullian), meaning “outer”.

phrases.latin: verba aut Latīna aut peregrīna sunt. Peregrīna porrō ex omnibus prope dīxerim gentibus ut hominēs, ut īnstitūta etiam multa vēnērunt.
phrases.english: Words are either Latin or foreign. And foreign words have come to us, I would almost say, from every nation, as people have, and many customs too.

phrases.latin: quae in hortīs nāscuntur, alia peregrīnīs vocābulīs, ut Graecīs ōcimum, menta, rūta
phrases.english: of the plants that grow in gardens, some have foreign names, Greek ones, like ocimum, menta, ruta

sources: Lewis & Short: externus · Lewis & Short: peregrinus · Lewis & Short: alienigena · Lewis & Short: exoticus
